problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$

examples.problem:
Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/07f01e2a202e29fee28a98d386df1d22fd21efcf1ee4d0a6a4cc56f9b637d57c.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/a547975b3524322daec753a8ddd010e50e815307d72bc07933d1e3674b4b462c.png) be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/53de45d6b1504ec53ca81471731b06ac5524a12230f0414553624c116a6f47c6.png)
Given that $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of ${\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}}.$
examples.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =4+5\textrm{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-5\text{i}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}-5\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(4+5\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = \textrm{i}x_1.
$$

So, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/b212192b142e9b4686a4d39e5957db5f3bfbca6283bfcb1d88a6fc57a4a27848.png)

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/65c073a60a27234349281e873958c2c9d54fb703331a4de23cc358a3eab1b232.png) 

Now, since $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda_1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\lambda_2=\overline{\lambda_1}=4-5\textrm{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $\mathbf v_1.$ Therefore, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/ca11ae0cca8d07c026108e71b96398171597f7330cb2390d871a8071e7bba873.png)

Finally, we obtain

$$
{\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}} = {\dfrac{(1)(1)}{(\textrm{i})(-\textrm{i})}} = 1.
$$

feedback.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3+\text{i} & -5 \\ 2 & 3+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(3+\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A+\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{5}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-3+\text{i}}{5}=-\frac{3}{5}+\frac{1}{5}\text{i}.$
